A pilgrimage is a journey made to a place that holds deep sacred, spiritual, or special significance to the person travelling there. It is not an ordinary trip for leisure or business. The traveller goes because the destination means something profound — and the act of going there itself is considered an important, meaningful deed.

The person who makes a pilgrimage is called a pilgrim.

Three things distinguish a pilgrimage from a regular journey:

1. A significant destination
The place being visited is not just interesting or beautiful — it is meaningful in a deeper sense. It might be a holy site, a sacred shrine, a place where something spiritually important happened, or a place connected to someone revered (a prophet, a saint, a spiritual teacher, or even an admired person).

2. A purpose rooted in devotion, reverence, or deep personal meaning
People go on pilgrimages to fulfil a religious duty, seek blessings, express gratitude, ask for forgiveness, pray for healing, honour the memory of someone, deepen their faith, or simply feel closer to something they hold sacred.

3. The journey itself is part of the act
Unlike a casual trip where only the destination matters, in a pilgrimage the travelling itself is often considered meaningful — even spiritually valuable. Many pilgrims undertake difficult or long journeys on purpose, because the effort, sacrifice, and hardship are seen as a form of devotion.

Pilgrimage is most strongly associated with religion, and nearly every major religion in the world has its own pilgrimages:

  • Islam: The Hajj — the annual pilgrimage to Mecca in Saudi Arabia — is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able is required to make this journey at least once in their lifetime. Millions of Muslims from around the world travel to Mecca together each year.
  • Hinduism: Pilgrimages are deeply woven into Hindu life. Famous ones include the Char Dham Yatra (visiting four sacred sites: Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, and Rameswaram), the Amarnath Yatra (a trek through the Himalayas to a sacred ice cave), and pilgrimages to the holy city of Varanasi on the banks of the Ganges. The Kumbh Mela — held every few years at sacred river confluences — draws the largest human gathering on Earth.
  • Christianity: Christians make pilgrimages to Jerusalem (where Jesus lived, died, and is believed to have risen), to Rome (the seat of the Pope and home to the Vatican), and to Santiago de Compostela in Spain (where the remains of the apostle Saint James are said to rest). Millions walk the famous Camino de Santiago route each year.
  • Buddhism: Buddhists travel to Bodh Gaya in India (where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under the Bodhi Tree), to Lumbini in Nepal (where the Buddha was born), and to other sites connected to his life.
  • Judaism: The Western Wall (also called the Wailing Wall) in Jerusalem is the holiest site in Judaism, and Jews from around the world travel there to pray.

While the word originates in religious practice, "pilgrimage" is also used more broadly to describe any deeply meaningful journey to a place that holds great personal or cultural significance — even when religion is not involved.

For example:

  • A fan of the writer Jane Austen travelling to her home in Chawton, England, and feeling moved and reverent upon arriving — that could be called a pilgrimage.
  • Someone visiting the birthplace of their favourite musician or poet as an act of admiration and tribute.
  • A person visiting the grave of a loved one or a historical figure they deeply respect.
  • Fans visiting the locations where their beloved films were made.

In all these cases, what matters is the sense of reverence, the significance of the destination, and the idea that going there means something beyond ordinary travel.

"Pilgrimage" is also used in a figurative sense — meaning it can describe a long, difficult, or meaningful journey toward something important even when it is not literal travel.

For example:

  • "His years of struggle and learning were a pilgrimage toward wisdom."
  • "She described her recovery from illness as a personal pilgrimage."

Here, "pilgrimage" captures the idea of a transformative, purposeful journey — whether physical or metaphorical.

It helps to understand what separates a pilgrimage from similar things:

  • A tourist trip is about seeing new places for enjoyment or curiosity. A pilgrimage is about devotion or deep personal meaning — not entertainment.
  • A regular commute or business travel has a practical goal. A pilgrimage's goal is spiritual, religious, or deeply personal.
  • A vacation is primarily about rest and pleasure. A pilgrimage often involves effort, sacrifice, or hardship willingly accepted.

A pilgrimage is a special, intentional journey to a place of sacred, spiritual, or deeply personal significance. It is motivated by devotion, reverence, religious duty, or a desire for spiritual meaning — not by practical need or casual interest. The journey itself is often considered as important as arriving at the destination. While most pilgrimages are religious in nature, the word is also used whenever someone travels to a place with deep personal meaning, or — figuratively — whenever someone undergoes a long, transformative journey toward something they cherish or seek.
